identity.title: Outlier Gradient Analysis: Efficiently Identifying Detrimental Training Samples for Deep Learning Models

problem.claim: Identify training samples that harm model performance.

gap.claim: Influence-function analysis is constrained for large deep models by the computational cost of inverting the Hessian.

contributions.claim: Establishes a connection between influence-function-based detrimental-sample identification and outlier gradient detection.
Provides a straightforward Hessian-free formulation and interprets the gradient’s role in sample impact.
Applies outlier gradient analysis to mislabeled-sample detection, data selection for NLP transformers, and influential-sample identification for LLM fine-tuning.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish their approach by transforming influence-based sample identification into outlier gradient analysis, yielding a Hessian-free formulation.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report systematic empirical validation of the approach’s hypothesis on synthetic datasets.
The authors report detecting mislabeled samples in vision models and selecting samples to improve NLP transformer performance.
The authors report extending the approach to influential-sample identification for LLM fine-tuning.

narrative_sequence.summary: Frames detrimental training-sample identification as a core data-centric learning challenge.
Positions influence functions as a useful framework but notes their Hessian-inversion cost for large deep models.
Bridges influence-based identification and outlier gradient detection through a Hessian-free formulation.
Reports synthetic validation, vision mislabeled-sample detection, NLP data selection, and LLM fine-tuning applications.

source_observation.claim: The abstract pairs a computational bottleneck with a reformulation that removes Hessian dependence, then traces the approach across several sample-selection tasks.

lessons.interpretation: A compact paper narrative can make a method’s motivation and transferability visible by linking one specific bottleneck, one mechanism-level reformulation, and bounded application settings.
lessons.application: Frame a proposed method by stating the limiting computation, the exact representation or approximation that replaces it, and the tasks used to test that reformulation.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the work has no clear bottleneck-replacement relationship or when application settings do not test the proposed mechanism.

unknowns: The abstract does not report quantitative results, baselines, dataset details, model scales, or evaluation conditions.
The claimed performance improvements and effectiveness are author-reported; the abstract does not provide enough detail to assess their magnitude or robustness.
